overview: This single-page Department of State “List of Papers” serves as an index to material filed under decimal 894A.014 concerning the territorial status, sovereignty, administration, and naming of Formosa/Taiwan. It points to a two-part memorandum containing a historical sketch and observations on Japanese administration and the Formosan population; a chronological outline prepared by Mr. Kerr of the Military Intelligence Service; a memorandum titled “THE SOVEREIGNITY OF FORMOSA”; and telegrams from Chungking concerning whether Chinese official circles preferred the English name “Formosa” or “Taiwan.” The sheet also records dates, internal routing notations, and cross-references to related State Department decimal files.

subfiles.title: List of Papers for Territory, Formosa, Taiwan (894A.014)
subfiles.about: An index sheet identifies and briefly describes papers concerning Formosa/Taiwan, including memoranda, telegrams, historical material, and sovereignty questions.
subfiles.summary: The sheet inventories records filed under 894A.014 and supplies abbreviated dates, origins, routing information, and related decimal-file references. Its most detailed entry describes a two-part memorandum covering Formosan history, Japanese administrative practices, and the character and attitudes of the island’s inhabitants, together with a chronology prepared by Mr. Kerr of MIS. It also notes Chungking telegrams about official Chinese preference for “Formosa” as the English name and lists a memorandum titled “THE SOVEREIGNITY OF FORMOSA.”

interest: The sheet is useful as a map of a larger wartime and early postwar documentary file, revealing which dimensions of the Taiwan question interested the State Department: sovereignty, historical claims, Japanese colonial rule, local political attitudes, and even English-language nomenclature. Particularly notable is the indication that Chinese officials preferred “Formosa” in English and the attribution of a Formosa chronology to George H. Kerr, later an important commentator on Taiwan. Although the indexed papers themselves are not reproduced here, the cross-references and terse descriptions can guide historians toward related records dispersed across several decimal-file classifications.
